raw.title: When Do Rankings Beat Signs? Gradient Direction Recovery under Even Nuisance
raw.body: Can ranking a batch of antipodal query pairs recover a gradient direction with fewer evaluations than using within-pair signs alone? We study fixed-center recovery in $d$ dimensions for a linear signal plus an unknown differentiable even nuisance, counting function evaluations and feedback rounds separately. Shared pair offsets create an information hierarchy: Mirror retains within-pair signs, Reverse couples reversed cross-pair orders to cancel offsets, and Full enforces all ranking inequalities. Relative shell variation is the nuisance range over the query sphere normalized by the linear-signal scale. When it is at most $c\varepsilon/\sqrt{d}$, Reverse localizes every consistent direction to angular accuracy $\varepsilon$ using $\widetilde{O}(d+\sqrt{d/\varepsilon})$ evaluations in one round at fixed confidence, without a variation bound supplied to the decoder. This matches a lower bound up to logarithmic factors, versus the $Θ(d/\varepsilon)$ one-round sign-only minimax cost on the same class. Over well-conditioned positive-definite quadratics with no common relative-curvature bound, the $R$-round minimax cost is instead $Θ(dR(\varepsilon^{-1/R}-1))$, even with cumulative rankings. We extend validity beyond exact evenness under supplied error bounds. Matched-endpoint experiments certify information beyond signs and short cycles. On two ridge tasks under joint evaluation and round caps, short-cycle recovery attains lower terminal mean gaps than the tested batch-capable controls. An additional optimization benefit from fitting the complete ranking remains unestablished.

raw.body:
# When Can You Ship on Offline Evals Alone?

![Feature Image](https://images.ctfassets.net/p762jor363g1/4w1jduYhnyiLjUjI8Ar3ZH/e354d444350d376d11dbde38a9213272/2.1__1_.png)

**TL;DR** *Teams building AI features want to skip slow A/B tests and decide from offline evals alone. This post looks at when that’s possible while keeping the risk of harming the online metric low. It can work, but only under strong assumptions that are hard to verify and can change over time. Noise is a problem too, because it can hide a strong link between offline and online results. In our example, a naive estimate says the eval explains 24% of the variation in online results, when the true figure is 60%.*

As agentic and LLM-based products and features become increasingly common, there is growing discussion about how to iterate on them efficiently. To assess product quality and the impact of changes, offline evals have become a standard part of the toolkit, alongside human evaluations, online A/B tests, and surveys.

When we change an AI feature, say a new prompt or a different underlying LLM, there are two main ways to check whether it got better. Offline evals are quick tests run on a fixed set of sample prompts before any real user sees the change, often with other LLM-as-judges grading the answers. A/B tests give the new version to a random group of real users and compare how they behave against users on the old version.

A question that frequently comes up is whether we can rely more heavily on offline evals and less on alternatives that are more time-consuming and resource-intensive. More specifically, *can we skip A/B tests and rely only on offline evals to make product decisions?* And if so, when?

The potential upside is substantial. Offline evals take hours; A/B tests often take days or weeks.

If we could confidently make product decisions based on offline evals alone, we could shorten feedback loops and iterate much faster. But what exactly do we mean by *“can* we make decisions on evals alone”?

![Figure 1](//images.ctfassets.net/p762jor363g1/4JjjfhoP5DUhFU06MmME7O/2aa56a7be9fd8cdc5a736c1d6abf118f/Figure_1.png)


Figure 1: The idealistic decision flow with offline evals and an A/B test in sequence for each product decision.

The goal of this post is twofold. First, to formalize what guarantees we would want from a decision to ship a change based on offline evals, without an A/B test.

Second, to understand what we need to know, assume, or estimate to achieve such a guarantee, and the major challenges and pitfalls involved.

In our paper, [When Can You Ship on Evals Alone?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10142), we work through this problem in detail. The approach is general and aims to help build intuition for any team building LLM-based products.

## What do we need to know?

We formalize the “when we can ship based on eval alone” as follows: *We want to make shipping decisions based on the offline eval while bounding the risk of shipping something that actually harms the online metric.*

If we want to bound the risk of shipping something that harms the online metric, ideally we need to know the conditional distribution of the true online treatment effect, given the observed offline eval treatment effect. If we know this distribution, we can directly assess and bound the risk of making a harmful shipping decision given any observed eval effect. In plain terms: for any eval result, we want to know how likely it is that the change actually helps or hurts real users, in terms of some specific online metric.

![Figure 2](//images.ctfassets.net/p762jor363g1/7oR6tYsGJV1M28QWttJNRS/2c84f5c6cd5036c84433145e623b6cd4/Figure_2.png)


Figure 2: the joint distribution of observed offline eval effects and true online effects. The “slice” at any given eval effect is the conditional distribution of the true online effect given the observed offline effect.

So how can we learn this relationship? This is where things get nuanced.

The first challenge is that we need paired observations of offline eval effects and online treatment effects, all coming from the same underlying relationship. We cannot have a heterogeneous set of experiments where, for some types of changes, an improvement in the eval corresponds to an improvement in the online outcome, while for others the relationship is different or even reversed.

The second challenge is measurement error. Both numbers are noisy estimates, not exact values. Offline eval scores have sampling errors from several sources, including randomly sampling examples from a larger eval set, and using an LLM to grade the answers (LLM-as-a-judge). Online treatment effects are estimated with sampling error too. We need to account for these errors when learning the relationship.
